author: D.M. Martins Research
title: My 3 Favorite Investment Strategies For 2019
text:
2019 is here. Not since the end of the Great Recession has the S&P 500 ( SPY ) finished a year substantially in the red while enduring high levels of volatility, making some investors wonder whether the end of the long bull cycle could mean that an even rougher 2019 lurks on the horizon.
On my end, I continue to support the views that making short-term predictions is a futile exercise. As I presented early in 2018 , a coin flip has been historically and statistically more accurate at anticipating market performance than Wall Street experts have. Given the unknowns and not any unusual ability that I may have at predicting the future, I believe a balanced and cautious approach here is highly advisable.
In this article, I present in detail my three favorite investment strategies for 2019. I expect to have all my longer-term nest egg invested in a combination of them.
Credit: iMoney
#1: Collecting dividends and option premiums I have been writing quite a bit lately about buy-write (also known as covered call) strategies. Simply put, the approach consists of:
Holding a long equity position, ideally in high-yielding stocks; selling short-dated calls on the reference asset to enhance yield in the portfolio; and (optionally) buying long-dated, out-of-the-money puts for some level of downside protection.
Let me break down each of the three steps presented above.
Long equities : this is the base of the portfolio. Ideally, the stock investment should be (1) diversified, better yet if weighed less heavily towards the S&P 500-dominant tech and financial services sectors (revisit my discussion on this subject from about a year ago), and (2) concentrated on dividend payers with a healthy business model and solid balance sheet.
The idea here is for the success of the investment strategy to not be too dependent on the market value of stocks rising over the next 12 months - a speculative presumption, in my view. By investing in good companies that pay a reliable dividend, at least investors can count on pocketing a modest amount represented by the stocks' blended dividend yield, possibly reinvesting or "dripping" the cash back into the portfolio
Short individual stock calls : this is where the bulk of the annual returns in a buy-write strategy would come from (between two-thirds and three-fourths of the total is a good estimate). By selling covered calls, investors give up upside potential in the stock that they own in exchange for an option premium payment that can often be quite hefty.
Here, I would suggest frequent options sales for the more "hands-on" investor. Contracts that expire sooner tend to be priced higher per unit of time (e.g. per day) than those that expire farther in the future - primarily due to the nature of volatility. To illustrate this point very simply, an ATM (at-the-money) call option contract on Apple ( AAPL ) with an expiration date of December 31st, 2019 sold for $655 on January 2nd (see left table below). Meanwhile, an ATM contract with an expiration date of January 17th, 2020 sold for $1,925 (right table). For about 12 months of "extra coverage", the long-dated option was worth only three times more than the short-dated instrument.
Source: DM Martins Research, using option tables from e-Trade
Notice that selling a series of short-dated contracts and rolling them throughout the course of the year should result in higher premiums collected than doing so with long-dated options. Needless to say, selling high is generally a desirable outcome in any investment strategy. Remember, however, that the more active approach may come at the expense of even more limited upside opportunity, higher trading fees and more diligence required to regularly maintain the portfolio.
Long broad market puts : this is the downside protection feature of the strategy. Given the uncertainty in the markets as of late, I find it interesting to have some insurance against sizable losses, should the economy begin to deteriorate in 2019.
Keep in mind that the equities portfolio described in the first step above should be diversified enough to resemble the broad market to some capacity. Therefore, buying long-dated puts on the S&P 500 should be good enough a move (even if not a perfect one) to protect the portfolio as a whole from dipping too far.
Also, remember that long-dated options cost less on a per-time-unit basis than their short-dated counterparts. Here, I would probably use some of the money raised through call option selling (step #2 above) to cover the cost of an out-of-the-money protective put. Today, a one-year long hedge against losses of 10% or more in SPY costs about 4.2% of a portfolio's total value, suggesting a fairly high implied volatility of 23%.
I have recently presented a trade idea on network equipment provider Nokia ( NOK ) that very closely resembles the full approach described above. One main difference is that the protective put in that particular case was on the individual stock itself rather than on the broad market - making the "insurance" against losses more expensive. The chart below depicts the possible outcomes from a $10,000 NOK trade. Notice how the strategy still provides unlimited upside (albeit with slightly lower expected returns than the straight ownership of the stock) coupled with desirable downside protection.
Source: DM Martins Research, using data from e-Trade
Those who do not have the time, patience or investment sophistication to assemble a buy-write portfolio and do not care as much about control over expected returns and stock selection may be best served by ETFs. I have covered a few of the top ones, and found out that the Horizons NASDAQ 100 Covered Call fund ( QYLD ) might (1) be the best alternative in the buy-write space and (2) perform better than the equities benchmark in most market environments - with the 2009-2017 raging bull being a notable exception.
#2: The good old 60/40, modified For quite a while, I have believed in preparing for whatever might happen in the markets through diversification across non-risk free asset classes. This is one of the key investment lessons that I have kept from my Bridgewater Associates years, particularly in what pertains to the hedge fund's "All Weather" strategy (I have previously written more on the subject).
Many investors may know about and have even followed this approach through the traditional "60/40 portfolio" made up of 60% diversified equities and 40% diversified bonds. I believe this is a good start, but also think that a few tweaks to the allocation may be helpful for those with a long-term investment horizon in mind.
First, most "balanced" portfolios tend to be unbalanced from a risk perspective. As I presented in more detail back in December, stocks tend to be much more volatile than fixed income instruments, aside from speculative high-yield bonds in some cases. Therefore, under stormy conditions similar to what we saw in the fourth quarter of last year, the ups and downs of stocks tend to drag along with it the performance of the portfolio as a whole - which does not help to provide much diversification.
A good case study on the destructive power of volatility was 1987. The chart below depicts the performance of $10,000 invested in a 60/40 portfolio (blue line) from January 1987 to December 1987. The seemingly diversified and balanced portfolio did not perform very well during the more bearish and volatile period of time, as outlined below:
Flat annual return (i.e. zero) vs. the S&P 500's +3% and Treasuries' -3% Annual volatility of 19% vs. the S&P 500's 30% and Treasuries' 10% Correlation of 1.0 with the S&P 500
Source: Portfolio Visualizer
To reduce a portfolio's exposure to equity risks and keep correlations lower, I believe a heavier allocation towards bonds would be necessary. For example, a 40/60 portfolio is better balanced than its 60/40 cousin from a risk-adjusted perspective (notice the subtle difference), even if the expected absolute return of the former might trail that of the latter in the long run. Considering that volatility in U.S. stocks has historically hovered around 15% against intermediate treasuries' 8%, a 35/65 split would likely be even more appropriate for the sake of maximizing risk-adjusted returns and protecting a portfolio against what could be a lingering bear market.
Investors interested in maintaining a healthier bond-to-equity ratio while boosting expected return might want to consider leveraging the portfolio's exposure to fixed income - a more sophisticated approach to balanced investing. The intended goal of using leverage here is to move bonds further up the risk-reward spectrum (i.e. turn them into higher risk, higher return instruments), therefore providing to the portfolio a viable balancing position to equities without much sacrifice to expected returns.
Source: graph provided by Above the Canopy
One of the instruments that I have identified to achieve the results outlined above is the Direxion Daily 7-10 Yr Treasury Bull 3X fund ( TYD ). I wrote more extensively about this ETF a month ago and observed that (contrary to popular belief and the prospectus itself) it produced more desirable results when held for the purpose of longer term investing rather than short-term trading.
Having said this, I should warn readers that leveraged strategies can cause severe damage to a portfolio if used improperly or irresponsibly, and meticulous due diligence is highly encouraged.
#3: Limited downside, unlimited upside My third and final strategy for 2019 is more of a variant of the second one above. Notice that my modified bonds/equities approach should be better balanced than the traditional 60/40 or an all-equities portfolio. But it still theoretically leaves the investment exposed to sizable losses - imagine, for example, a bad year for bonds and stocks alike, as economic growth slows down and inflation shoots higher along with interest rates.
For a very conservative version of a balanced portfolio, exposure to equities can be achieved through long call option positions alongside a primarily conservative fixed income position. Let me be clearer and more specific.
Take the following chart that illustrates the gains from $1 million invested in an S&P 500 ETF at different index prices, and compares it to the returns of 40 at-the-money call option contracts ($1 million divided by $250/share of SPY divided by 100 options per contract = 40 contracts) on the index with a maturity date of December 31st (i.e. roughly one year):
Source: DM Martins Research, using data from Yahoo Finance and e-trade
Notice that, to get 1x exposure to the S&P 500 with a $1 million investment, one might choose to buy $1 million worth of SPY - simple enough. To get the same exposure through options, one must pay an $80,360 premium to buy 40 contracts that, above the strike price of $250/share, will produce the same gains that a $1 million investment in SPY would generate.
Market returns with only a fraction of the principal invested: this sounds a bit like leverage, doesn't it? Better yet, a drop in SPY below the strike price of $250 would not result in portfolio losses beyond the premium disbursed for the call options.
A "limited downside, unlimited upside" portfolio like this can probably be very simply invested in (2) treasuries at 92% allocation, yielding 2.7%, and (2) at-the-money call options on SPY representing 8% of the total amount invested (see pie chart below). Under no circumstances would this nest egg lose more than 5.3% of its total value (8% paid on options minus 2.7% yield on treasuries), assuming the government bonds are held to maturity. And while a largely sideways-moving market might leave the portfolio slightly in the red, the investment would still fully participate in an eventual recovery in the S&P 500 as if 100% of the portfolio had been allocated to equities.
Source: DM Martins Research
Parting words Will stocks have a better year in 2019 than they did in 2018? I do not know for sure, and I am pretty confident that almost all Wall Street gurus have no clue either (regardless of how confident they might sound on TV).
Therefore, I find it much smarter and more reasonable to take a cautious stance towards investing amid all the uncertainties. As 2019 kicks off, I encourage readers to focus primarily on portfolio strategies that can produce rich returns in a bullish scenario while staying protected from sizable losses in the event of another bear attack.
